topic: Housing Price Index (HPI): a price chart for houses, how buyers, sellers, brokers, banks, economists and government use it, and India's two main indices (NHB RESIDEX and RBI's HPI) with primary vs secondary market

book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook would define HPI, explain how it is built (base year, index value, which transactions) and then list its uses and publishers. This video starts from a familiar decision (is now the right time to buy this share?) and its familiar tool (a price chart), asks the same question for a house, and gives HPI as the answer. It then spends most of its time on who uses the index and why, each use told as a small story (a seller waiting, a broker overcharging, a bank stuck with an overpriced house), and only at the end names India's two indices and the transactions they cover. How an index number is calculated or read is never taught.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Introduce the tool through a decision the learner already knows, then cut the topic by user: one user, one problem the index solves for that user.

narration.density: About 25 terms (share, stock price chart, invest, HPI, residential real estate, buyer, seller, informed decision, housing market, broker, money lender, financial institution, housing loan, documents, default, area rate, economist, consumer behaviour, policy maker, economic policy, NHB, RESIDEX, RBI, central bank, primary market, secondary market) in about 273 s, about 5.5 per minute, at the fastest speech of the three (about 187 words per minute). Most terms are everyday and carried by small stories, so class 9 up can follow; the NHB/RBI comparison at the end is dense and text-only, and the word 'index' is never unpacked (no index value, no base year).

talmel_summary: Only the first 36 s have tiles: after that the red line inside the HPI badge redraws on a loop, so the change detector reads one continuous change to the end and no later tiles exist. In the hook the picture leads the voice by 2-3 s (the question written before it is asked, the chart before 'ye chart', the house before 'ghar'), which works for a hook. Checked on the 10 s keyframes instead, the later additions (definition, buyers/sellers, broker photo, user spokes, each green tick, the two logos, the [2007] tags and the two callouts) fall within the 10 s window of their words, but the long stories (the seller waiting, the broker, the bank's default case, primary vs secondary) are told over a still picture, and the looping line never falls when 'HPI is down' is said.

voice.notes: About 187 words per minute, the fastest of this batch, with few pauses; friendly direct address ('agar main aapse poochhoon', 'aap apna ghar bechna chahte hain') and second-person stories. Stress on 'sahi samay' in the hook and on 'loss' in each story. The share price is read as '2544 rupees' (screen shows paise); years read in English (2007). The lenders' story speeds up and runs as one long chain without a pause for the learner.

game_ideas.player_does: Works as a bank's home-loan officer: each applicant brings a house, its asking price and the area's HPI line; the player approves or rejects the loan amount.
game_ideas.process_happens: Approved loans run forward a few years; some buyers default, the bank takes the documents, sells the house at the area's HPI price and the shortfall or surplus shows in the bank's vault.
game_ideas.win: Lend only up to the HPI-backed value, so every forced sale covers the loan.
game_ideas.lose: Approving an overpriced house shows the forced sale falling short and the vault losing money: the reason lenders check HPI.
game_ideas.concept: why lenders check HPI: the house as loan security

game_ideas.player_does: Owns a house and must sell within two years; each month sees the city's HPI line and a broker's offer, and decides to sell now or wait.
game_ideas.process_happens: The HPI line moves month by month; offers above the trend come from a pushy broker on the buying side, offers below it when the market is down.
game_ideas.win: Sell when the line is up and the offer matches the area value; spot a broker's inflated quote when buying the next house.
game_ideas.lose: Selling in a dip shows the loss against the trend; accepting the broker's inflated price on the next purchase shows how much was overpaid.
game_ideas.concept: HPI for buyers and sellers: informed decisions

game_ideas.player_does: Sorts house-sale cards (builder sells a new flat; family resells its flat; builder sells in a small town; owner resells in a metro) into primary and secondary market, then into the index that counts them as the video describes.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each card drops into its market bin; the two index badges light up for the sales they include.
game_ideas.win: All cards in the right market bin (developer to buyer = primary, owner to new buyer = secondary).
game_ideas.lose: A resale placed in 'primary' shows the developer missing from the deal; keep the index-coverage step marked 'check source' until verified.
game_ideas.concept: NHB vs RBI coverage; primary vs secondary market

checks_learned: A decorative loop (the line redrawing inside the badge) must not run under explanations: motion must mean something, e.g. the line falls when 'HPI is down' is said; a looping animation also blinds the change detector that BIE's own talmel check needs.
A spoken scenario with steps (loan, documents held, default, sale, shortfall) must be drawn step by step; adding a tick is not showing.
Real company names, real share prices and real charts may not be used as hooks; use a made-up company and avoid anything that reads as buy or sell advice.
Real people's photos must not stand in for characters (the broker), and a profession must not be drawn as a villain.
Facts about institutions' roles must be date-checked (NHB's regulatory role changed in 2019) and data-coverage claims checked against the publisher's method note.
Numbers on screen (2,544.95; chart axis and months) that are never spoken should be spoken or removed.
A video about an index must say what an index value means (base 100, a rise to 120 = prices up 20%); flag 'index' topics with no index number.
A definition given only in callout text (primary vs secondary market) needs its picture (developer -> buyer vs owner -> new buyer).

teaching_best.why: Hook through a decision the learner knows (is this the right time to buy?) and its known tool (a price chart); HPI arrives as the answer to the learner's own question for houses.
A concrete what-if for one user (seller in no hurry, HPI down, wait, avoid loss) turns 'informed decision' into an action.
A misconception line ('not only buyers and sellers') opens the second half and the list of other users.
The lender's risk is reasoned step by step (overpriced house, default, sale falls short) before the conclusion that banks check HPI.
Primary vs secondary market is defined by who sells to whom, which is easy to picture.

teaching_weak.why: The hook uses a real company and its real share price and chart; it can read as stock advice.
'Index' is never unpacked: no index value, no base year, no example of reading a rise or fall in numbers.
The best mechanism (the bank's default case) and the seller's example are told over a still picture.
The broker is a villain-style photo of a real person: stereotype and real likeness.
NHB called the home-loan regulator (outdated since 2019) and the NHB/RBI coverage split may not match the indices' methods; verify.
No recap of the users or the two indices and no exam link.
